Senses.Explanation: To raise or hold upright the whisk, the teaching-seat implement and emblem of authority. The action occurs as an answer, demonstration, and object of public questioning rather than as a gesture with one fixed message. Nanta Guangyong answers a question about Manjusri's teacher by raising the whisk. Zhaozhou Congshen raises it when asked whether he will receive the person who sets the realm in order. Yuanwu Keqin twice raises it and says, "Just this is it." Yunmen Wenyan reopens an older exchange in which a monk asks Zifu Zhensui the import of the ancients picking up the mallet and raising the whisk. Deshan Yuanming classifies raising a finger and raising the whisk as a dead phrase. In the dominant spelling, Baiyu Jingsi raises the whisk and asks whether the assembly sees, while Yinyuan Longqi raises it as his answer to a new-command question and then tests the monk's shouts. The Zen bend is the action's institutional and interview setting: it is the presiding master's implement raised as an answer or challenge, while the corpus refuses a universal symbolic decoding. Xueyan Zuqin twice raises the whisk within hall addresses—once before calling unfreed affective dust blindness, and once before a moon verse. The surrounding sayings differ, but the referent remains the same public action with the teaching-seat implement.
Senses.Note: The frozen allowlisted corpus has 584 exact hits of the seeded spelling in 109 files / 105 works and 2,598 hits of the dominant spelling in 267 files / 263 works. Nine anchors cover direct answers, repeated demonstration, a raised old case, critical classification, and two governed dominant-spelling variants. The two spellings are readings of the same action, never separate senses.
